Research note

Shuffling the Frames

A Simple Investigation into Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Tracks for BCI

Amulya Harish · October 2026 · 4 min read

How I came across the data

At the Axo Neurotech hackathon in August, I spent the day with friends automating Flappy Bird gameplay with EMG, but the talk I kept thinking about was Lev Chizhov's on the future of ultrasound in neurotech. His company, Aleph Neuro, wants brain interfaces you can wear: ultrasound images of blood flow, decoded by models trained on very large datasets, the way MindEye decodes what people see from fMRI. Lev shared two recordings at the hackathon, and Aleph has open-sourced the pipeline that turns them into maps of blood flow. I wanted to explore the data and build on top of it.

The recordings image a human brain through the skull, about a minute through the temple and half a minute through the back of the head. Microbubbles injected into the blood echo brightly, and the pipeline links each bubble from frame to frame into tracks that trace the vessels. Below are the tracks from the temple recording.

The test: shuffle the frames

Before improving anything, I wanted to know how many tracks were real. Shuffling is a method I use in my lab at USC to compare a data processing step against a null: scramble the one thing a real result depends on, and see what survives. Here that thing is time. I put the frames in a random order and ran the same tracker again. Every bright spot is still there, but a real bubble can no longer be followed, so any track that still appears is chance. Comparing the two counts shows how much of the output is real.

What the shuffle found

With the settings Aleph's guide recommends (tracks of 5 or more points, real order against shuffled):

  • Temple, first 28 seconds: 193 against 199. Essentially all chance.
  • Temple, last 28 seconds: 675 against 9. Almost all real.
  • Back of head: 1,261 against 861. About two thirds chance throughout.

Early in the temple recording few bubbles had reached the brain, and the brightest thing in most frames was one spot just under the skull that flickers constantly. Almost all the early tracks sit on it, and a spot that never moves can be "followed" in any frame order. Later, more bubbles arrived and real tracks took over.

The deeper cause is that the tracker uses one brightness threshold for the whole picture, while signal and noise both fade about tenfold between 1 and 5.5 cm deep. Near the skull the threshold sits just below the noise, so noise becomes chance tracks. Below 3 cm it sits 3 to 7 times above the noise, so real bubbles are missed: fake bubbles I planted 4 to 6 cm deep, six times brighter than the noise, were never found. A plain track count hides all of this, and is easy to inflate; the shuffled count gives every run a chance level to beat.

A possible fix

Even out the depth before detection: scale each depth so the background noise sits at the same level everywhere, like the depth sliders on a hospital ultrasound machine, so one threshold means the same thing at every depth. Aleph's pipeline has a formula for this but applies it before the clutter filter that removes the steady echo of skull and tissue. I applied the same formula after the filter and changed nothing else. Counting tracks that travel (at least 10 points and 2 mm, mostly in one direction) over both full recordings:

Tracks below 3 cm (chance in brackets)TempleBack of head
As shared54 (2)13 (0)
With the fix172 (4)248 (0)
Tracks above 3 cm kept76%77%

Planted deep bubbles went from never found to about 90% found. Applying the correction before the filter, as the pipeline does now, keeps only about half of the shallow tracks.

So my suggestions to Aleph are to report a shuffled count next to every track count, and to apply the depth correction after the clutter filter. Both should carry over to imaging without bubbles, where the signal is weaker and still fades with depth. The limits: two recordings from one person, and shuffling catches chance links but not clutter that flickers in place for a second, which is why the table counts only tracks that travel.
